sitting.name: Ron DeSantis
sitting.title: Governor of Florida
sitting.address: Office of Governor Ron DeSantis, The Capitol, 400 S. Monroe St., Tallahassee, FL 32399-0001
sitting.notes: Not on the 2026 ballot; Art. IV, Sec. 5(b) bars a person who has served more than six years in two consecutive terms from election to the succeeding term. The sitting Lieutenant Governor is Jay Collins, appointed by DeSantis and sworn in Aug. 12, 2025 (source wlrn_lg); Collins sought the Republican nomination for governor and was eliminated in the Aug. 18, 2026 primary (source dos_canlist), so he is not on the general election ballot.

positions.text: Insurance: curb lawsuit abuse, cut state fees when reserves are full, keep Citizens Insurance small, and create an industry-funded online scorecard comparing insurers on price, claim speed and denial rates.

Permitting and taxes: post business, building and road permits online with enforced deadlines, create a single state permit hub, keep Florida's personal income tax at zero and require a balanced budget every year.
Health care: require doctors and hospitals to post guaranteed cash prices for the 50 most common tests and procedures, and require insurers to approve common treatments within three days.
Education: phonics-based teacher training and K-2 reading screening, paid apprenticeships through a 'LaunchPad Florida' program, and education funding that follows the student.

Immigration and crime: mandatory E-Verify for all Florida businesses, end state benefits that he says draw illegal immigration, and have state and local police work with federal agencies to deport noncitizens who commit crimes.

Insurance and housing costs: create a state catastrophic fund to take natural-disaster risk off private insurers, aiming to lower property and car insurance rates, and offer no-interest state-backed loans to condo associations and owners.
Health care: expand Medicaid.

Public schools: substantially increase public school funding and teacher pay; require voucher-funded private schools to meet public school standards, bar them from charging extra tuition, and means-test the voucher program.
Data centers: an immediate moratorium on building hyperscale data centers until environmental, water and community impacts are studied.
Ethics: campaign finance reform and a broad ethics package focused on transparency.
Stop taxing homeowners on their homesteads (the page does not specify a mechanism).
Address high homeowner insurance premiums (no specific mechanism given).
Education money should follow the child; parents decide what is best for their children.
Secure the border and open a lawful path to work, with enforcement focused on criminals and traffickers.
Smaller government: make the state live on a budget and end waste, fraud and special deals.
Eliminate property tax on homesteaded homes worth up to twice the county median, and stop corporations from buying up single-family homes.
Insurance: cap insurer profits, require plain-language rate filings and whole-company accounting, and restore the right to sue over wrongly denied claims.
Health care: close the coverage gap for about 800,000 Floridians, start bulk drug importation and make care prices public.
Ban new AI data centers, end their subsidies and special rate deals, and keep residential ratepayers from covering their power costs.
End warrantless mass tracking by license plate reader networks; suspend state gas taxes during price spikes and remove tolls once a road's bonds are retired.

measures.title: Budget Stabilization Fund
measures.placedBy: Florida Legislature (legislative joint resolution HJR 5019, 2025; House 100-1, Senate 29-4)
measures.ballotSummary: Proposing an amendment to the State Constitution to increase the amount of funds that may be retained in the budget stabilization fund from 10% to 25% of general revenue collections, require the legislature to transfer the lesser of $750 million or the amount required to reach 25% of the general revenue collections each year unless certain conditions are met, and allow the legislature to withdraw funds for critical state needs.
measures.plain: Florida keeps a savings account, often called the rainy day fund, for emergencies and budget shortfalls. Today it can hold up to 10% of the state's general revenue. This amendment would raise the limit to 25%, require lawmakers to put in up to $750 million each year until the fund reaches that limit (with some exceptions), and let them take money out for 'critical state needs' with a two-thirds vote once the fund is above 15%.
measures.yesMeans: A YES vote means the rainy day fund limit rises from 10% to 25% of general revenue, with required yearly deposits of up to $750 million and a new way to withdraw money for critical state needs.
measures.noMeans: A NO vote means the fund limit stays at 10% of general revenue and the Constitution does not require yearly deposits.
measures.fiscal: No official financial impact statement is printed for this amendment; Florida's Financial Impact Estimating Conference prepares statements only for citizen-initiative amendments. The Senate bill summary says the Legislature would have to transfer $750 million a year until the fund reaches the new cap, with withdrawals allowed for critical needs only after the balance reaches 15% and never below 10% of revenue collections.
measures.supporters: Senate President Ben Albritton said it 'makes Florida's balance sheet more durable in difficult times.' The Republican Party of Florida says it 'makes sure Florida saves in good years so it doesn't have to raise taxes in bad ones.' Democratic governor nominee David Jolly supports it; Florida TaxWatch leans yes with reservations about long-term required payments.
measures.opponents: Gov. Ron DeSantis called it 'a foolish constitutional amendment proposal,' arguing the fund is already at its limit and surplus money should go to tax cuts. Rich Templin of the Florida AFL-CIO questioned moving money into savings while many needs are unmet. Republican governor nominee Byron Donalds and Americans for Tax Reform also oppose it.

measures.title: Exemption of Tangible Personal Property on Agricultural Land from Taxation
measures.placedBy: Florida Legislature (legislative joint resolution HJR 1215, 2025; House 110-1, Senate 37-0)
measures.ballotSummary: Proposing an amendment to the State Constitution to exempt tangible personal property habitually located or typically present on land classified as agricultural, used in the production of agricultural products or for agritourism activities, and owned by the landowner or leaseholder of the agricultural land from ad valorem taxation. If approved this amendment would first apply for tax years beginning January 1, 2027.
measures.plain: Businesses in Florida pay local property tax on equipment and other movable property, though the first $25,000 is already exempt. This amendment would fully exempt that kind of property, such as farm machinery and tools, when it is kept on land classified as agricultural, used for farming or agritourism, and owned by the landowner or leaseholder. The Legislature would set the details, and it would start with the 2027 tax year.
measures.yesMeans: A YES vote means equipment and other tangible personal property used on agricultural land for farming or agritourism would be exempt from local property taxes starting in 2027.
measures.noMeans: A NO vote means this property stays under current tax rules, including the existing $25,000 exemption for tangible personal property.
measures.fiscal: No official financial impact statement is printed for this legislatively referred amendment. The state Revenue Estimating Conference estimated that, if approved, it would reduce local government revenue by $31.0 million per year (recurring), beginning in fiscal year 2027-28.
measures.supporters: Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson says it ends 'the burdensome multiple taxation of agricultural production.' The Republican Party of Florida says it gives financial relief to farmers and agricultural businesses. Florida TaxWatch supports it.
measures.opponents: State Rep. Anna Eskamani (D) argued it lacks safeguards against windfalls and would mostly benefit a few large agribusinesses. The Sun Sentinel editorial board called it 'bad policy to enshrine special-interest tax breaks in the constitution.'

measures.title: Increased Homestead Exemption; Lower Cap on Increases in Non-Homestead Property Assessments
measures.articleRef: Article VII, Sections 4, 6 and 9; Article XII
measures.placedBy: Florida Legislature (legislative joint resolution CS/HJR 1-F, 2026 special session; House 75-26, Senate 30-9). The ballot title and summary were rewritten by the Attorney General and released Aug. 13, 2026, after Leon County Circuit Judge David Frank ruled the original wording defective.
measures.ballotSummary: This amendment increases the homestead exemption, for all non-school taxes, to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, and adjusts for inflation thereafter. It requires the Legislature to prescribe a uniform procedure for counties and municipalities, for their respective levies, to increase the homestead exemption up to full assessed value, and allows special districts, subject to referendum approval, to do the same. Persons who are not Florida residents on December 31, 2026, will receive the existing homestead exemption upon qualifying for a homestead exemption, with the increased homestead exemption beginning with the fifth year of exemption, to the extent permitted by the U.S. Constitution. This amendment reduces the annual cap on assessment increases for non-homestead properties from 10% to 5%. This amendment requires counties and municipalities to use property taxes solely for public safety, education and schools, infrastructure, natural resources, bond debt service, retirement benefits for employees, and operations and administration. Other expenditures may be approved by county officers or county or municipal governing bodies unless prohibited by general law, notwithstanding Article VII, Section 9(a) of the Florida Constitution, which allows counties and municipalities to levy property taxes for their respective purposes. This amendment takes effect January 1, 2027.
measures.plain: Today, Florida homeowners get up to $50,000 taken off their home's taxable value. This amendment would raise that to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 for all property taxes except school taxes, with inflation increases after that; people who move to Florida after 2026 would wait until their fifth year for the larger amount. It would also lower the yearly limit on assessment increases for non-homestead property, like rentals and businesses, from 10% to 5%, and limit what counties and cities can spend property tax money on.
measures.yesMeans: A YES vote means a larger homestead exemption for non-school taxes, a 5% yearly cap on assessment increases for non-homestead property, and new limits on how counties and cities may spend property tax revenue, starting Jan. 1, 2027.
measures.noMeans: A NO vote means the current homestead exemption, the 10% cap on non-homestead assessment increases, and current local spending rules stay in place.
measures.fiscal: No official financial impact statement is printed for this legislatively referred amendment. The state Revenue Estimating Conference (July 10, 2026) estimated that, if approved, local government property tax revenue would be lower by about $4.93 billion in FY 2027-28, $8.71 billion in FY 2028-29, $9.65 billion in FY 2029-30 and $10.71 billion in FY 2030-31, with a recurring annual impact of about $11.83 billion. The estimate does not include possible future local actions to raise exemptions further. School taxes are not affected.
measures.supporters: Gov. Ron DeSantis, CFO Blaise Ingoglia and Rep. Toby Overdorf, who led the House effort, support it, arguing it gives taxpayers relief and that local governments can cut waste. Florida Realtors and the James Madison Institute also support it.
measures.opponents: The Florida League of Cities, Florida Association of Counties, Florida Professional Firefighters, Florida State Fraternal Order of Police, Florida Sheriffs Association, 1000 Friends of Florida, Florida Policy Institute and the Save Our Services campaign oppose it, citing possible cuts to public safety and other local services and a shift of costs to renters and businesses. Florida TaxWatch recommends a no vote, saying the measure reached the ballot too quickly.

measures.title: Justice of the Supreme Court: Shall Justice Carlos G. Muñiz of the Supreme Court be retained in office?
measures.placedBy: Required merit retention vote for a sitting Florida Supreme Court justice (nonpartisan). Muñiz was appointed by Gov. Ron DeSantis on Jan. 22, 2019; his current term expires Jan. 5, 2027.
measures.ballotSummary: Shall Justice Carlos G. Muñiz of the Supreme Court be retained in office?
measures.thresholdNote: Not a constitutional amendment. The justice is retained unless a majority of voters vote No; the exact wording of the threshold was not verified from an official source.
measures.plain: Florida Supreme Court justices are appointed by the governor and then face a yes-or-no vote to stay in office. Justice Muñiz is on the ballot for a new six-year term. There is no opponent.
measures.yesMeans: A YES vote means Justice Muñiz stays on the Florida Supreme Court for another six-year term.
measures.noMeans: A NO vote means you want Justice Muñiz removed; if a majority vote No, a new justice would be chosen.
